cover_design.ringkas: A self-study course in Swahili for complete beginners — from saying hello in Zanzibar to telling the story of a trip you've just made.

product.title: Swahili 101 - A1 (English Edition)
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from zero to A1 Swahili: short dialogues, word-for-word translations that show how Swahili packs a whole sentence into one word, grammar notes, vocabulary with an English-friendly pronunciation guide, exercises, and an answer key. Swahili is kinder to beginners than its reputation: the spelling is perfectly regular, the stress always falls on the second-to-last syllable, nouns have no masculine/feminine gender, there are no articles, and plenty of words already sound familiar (safari, hoteli, daktari, basi, polisi). Each unit targets one of the spots that actually trip learners up, from the noun classes that set the tone of the whole sentence to the Swahili clock, which runs six hours apart from yours.

blocks.text: There is one sentence to read before anything else: **Swahili is spelled exactly the way it sounds**. The letter *a* is always "ah", *i* is always "ee", *u* is always "oo". No silent letters, no vowels that change with their neighbors, no historical spellings to memorize one by one like *through*, *though* and *thought*. You can read a Swahili sentence correctly within five minutes, and that is not a figure of speech — it really happens.

The second gift is waiting in the translation column. Point at any word on any page and there is a fair chance it has a story you half know. *Safari* is Swahili — English borrowed it, along with the Arabic *safar* (journey) behind it. *Habari* (news), *kitabu* (book), *wakati* (time), *dunia* (world) and hundreds more came from Arabic along the Indian Ocean trade routes. Then there is a second, more surprising group: *meza* (table), *bendera* (flag), *sabuni* (soap), left behind by Portuguese sailors. And a third one you will recognize at once: *basi*, *teksi*, *hoteli*, *daktari*, *polisi*, *benki*.

The third gift: **Swahili nouns have no gender**. No *der/die/das*, no *le/la*, and not even the articles *a* and *the* to weigh up every time you open your mouth. Even "he" and "she" are a single word, *yeye*.

So where is the hard part? In one place only, and this course won't pretend otherwise: **noun classes**. Swahili sorts its nouns into several classes, and the class sets the sound of the whole sentence — adjectives, demonstratives, possessives, even the verb prefix change their clothes to match. *Kitabu kizuri kimoja* (one good book) becomes *vitabu vizuri viwili* (two good books): one *ki-* turns into *vi-* and spreads to three words at once. For most learners this is the most foreign thing in Swahili. But there is an honest shortcut: the sound is contagious, so your ear will catch it long before your brain has finished memorizing the table.

The next piece of good news: **Swahili verbs don't conjugate like European verbs** — they are coupled together like train cars. *Ni-na-soma* = I-am-reading. Swap the middle car: *ni-li-soma* (I read, yesterday), *ni-ta-soma* (I will read), *ni-me-soma* (I have read). One pattern for every verb in the language, with almost no exceptions. You don't memorize twenty forms of *go*; you learn six subject prefixes and five tense slots, and then you can build thousands of sentences.

The twenty units are built in sequence, and each one adds a new peg while reusing all the earlier ones. You start by greeting someone at the port of Zanzibar and finish by telling the story of a trip, ordering dinner, bargaining at the market, explaining to a doctor where it hurts, and saying goodbye with sentences that sound like they come from someone who really lives there.

One last thing about who will understand you. Swahili is the bridge language of East Africa: official in Tanzania and Kenya, a national language in Uganda and eastern Congo, and spoken in Rwanda, Burundi, Zanzibar, the Comoros and coastal Mozambique. Estimates put its speakers at over two hundred million, and most of them use it as a second language — which means they are **used to hearing Swahili spoken with an accent**, patient with slow sentences, and almost always delighted to see you trying. Few major languages in the world are this welcoming to beginners. *Karibu.*

front.title: Contents
front.intro: This course works best in order — each unit reuses what the previous ones put in place.

blocks.text: Every unit has the same structure, and the order is not decoration — it is a way of learning that has been used for more than a century: **hear and understand first, rules later**.
1. Dialogue

Read the dialogue twice. First reading: cover the right-hand column and just try to catch the gist. Second reading: read the Swahili line, then its translation, then the **literal line** printed in small type underneath.

That literal line is the most important part of this course. It translates every piece of every word as it is, including the bits that sound odd in English. *Ninakupenda* is rendered "I-am-you-love", not "I love you". The oddness is the lesson: that is how Swahili really builds its sentences, and after ten units the pattern will feel natural without your ever having memorized it.
2. Notes and grammar

After the dialogue come short notes on what just happened, then one or two grammar boxes with tables. Don't memorize the tables. Read them, then go back to the dialogue and find the lines. A table you look at after recognizing the sentence sticks far longer than one memorized in advance.
3. Vocabulary

All the words from the unit are gathered in one three-column table: the Swahili spelling, **Say it**, and the meaning. The Say it column marks the stressed syllable in CAPITALS — *kee-TAH-boo*, *hah-BAH-ree*. Because Swahili stress almost always falls on the second-to-last syllable, you will soon be able to predict this column yourself. That is exactly the point.
4. Exercises and answer key

Four or five exercises close every unit, and the answer key comes right after them. Do them with a pen on a separate sheet, not in your head — a hand that writes remembers better than an eye that reads. On the Linguo dashboard you can also do these exercises on screen with automatic marking.
How long does a unit take?

One unit is designed for **one 30–45 minute session**, plus five minutes of rereading the next day. At one unit a day, twenty units take three weeks; at three units a week, seven weeks. Any pace is fine — the one thing not to do is skip units. Swahili stacks up, and unit 15 uses sounds set up in unit 6.

This section is short, and that is the good news. Swahili is written in the **Latin alphabet** and its spelling is almost perfectly honest: a letter is always read the same way, in every word, with no exceptions to memorize. Once you know the five vowels, you can read any Swahili sentence aloud.
Vowels: five, always pure

*a, e, i, o, u* are read **ah, eh, ee, oh, oo** — always short, always clear, never swallowed into the "uh" of English *about*. *Habari* is hah-BAH-ree, not h'BAH-ree. *Kutoka* is koo-TOH-kah, with three full vowels. Two things to watch: *e* is always the *e* of *bed*, never the *ee* of *see*; and *o* is a pure "oh" with no *w* glide at the end, as in Spanish or Italian.

In the **Say it** column, these vowels are spelled the English way so you never have to stop and think: *ah*, *eh*, *ee*, *oh*, *oo*. The Swahili text itself always keeps its normal spelling. Two vowels side by side are both pronounced, one after the other: *saa* (hour) = SAH-ah, *kuu* (main) = KOO-oo, *ndio* (yes) = n-DEE-oh.
Consonants that need attention

With the apostrophe, it is the *ng* of *singer*, even at the start of a word. Without it, *ng* is the *ng* of *finger*: *-ngapi* → NGAH-pee.

blocks.text: The rest fits in one breath: **sh** is as in *shop*, **j** as in *jam*, **y** as in *yes*, **w** as in *water*, and **h** is always pronounced — *hapa*, *hii*, *hodari*. The **r** is a light tap of the tongue, as in Spanish *pero* (or the *tt* of American *butter*); it often sounds almost like an *l*.
Consonant clusters at the start of a word

The one real surprise for an English tongue: Swahili words can begin with **mb-, nd-, nj-, ng-, mv-, nz-**, and with an **m** or **n** that stands alone as a syllable. *Mtu* (person) is m-TOO, with a quick hum of *m* before *tu*. *Ndizi* (banana) is n-DEE-zee. *Mzee* (elder) = m-ZEH-eh.

Don't slip in a helper vowel — it's *mtu*, not *muh-tu*. The trick: close your lips, hum *mmm* for a split second, then release the rest of the word. In words like *mtu* and *mkate*, that hum counts as a syllable of its own, which is why the stress lands where it might surprise you: *m-KAH-teh*.
The stress rule: one sentence

**Stress always falls on the second-to-last syllable.** Always. *hah-BAH-ree*, *kee-TAH-boo*, *ah-SAHN-teh*, *kah-REE-boo*, *nee-nah-SOH-mah*, *too-tah-oh-NAH-nah*. Because Swahili verbs grow longer as you add cars, the stress shifts back on its own — and you don't have to memorize anything for that. The Say it column marks it in capitals, but after a few units you'll stop looking.

front.title: Swahili words with a familiar ring

blocks.text: Before the first unit, take five minutes for this page. It holds Swahili words that come with a ready-made memory hook. Most arrived the same way: with Arab merchants and Portuguese sailors who stopped along the East African coast centuries ago.
From Arabic — several of them are English words too

The days of the week hold a surprise too: **Alhamisi** (Thursday) and **Ijumaa** (Friday) come straight from Arabic. The rest are easier still, because Swahili simply counts them: *Jumatatu* (day three = Monday), *Jumanne* (day four… = Tuesday — the count starts from Saturday), *Jumatano*, *Jumamosi*, *Jumapili*.
From Portuguese — and a few other ports of call

⚠️ Two small traps before you get too confident. *Kaka* means **older brother** — nothing more. And *mama* does mean mother, but in East Africa it is also a respectful way to address any adult woman, like "ma'am".

And the easiest group of all — English words in Swahili clothes: *basi* (bus), *teksi* (taxi), *treni* (train), *hoteli* (hotel), *daktari* (doctor), *polisi* (police), *benki* (bank), *tiketi* (ticket), *shati* (shirt), *baiskeli* (bicycle), *redio* (radio), *kompyuta* (computer). Add a vowel at the end, spell it as it sounds, and you have a Swahili word.
The whole course, condensed into a few tables. These pages are meant to be looked at after you've finished the units — not memorized up front.
Pronouns and subject prefixes

Numbers
Six numbers agree with their noun class (*-moja, -wili, -tatu, -nne, -tano, -nane*): *watu wawili*, *vitabu viwili*, *nyumba mbili*. The other four never change: *sita*, *saba*, *tisa*, *kumi*.
Question words

These forty verbs cover most of everyday conversation. The dictionary form always starts with *ku-* ("to…"), and that *ku-* drops off as soon as a subject prefix is attached — except in six one-syllable verbs that hold on to it (*kula*, *kunywa*, *kuja*, *kwenda*, *kuwa*, *kufa*).

blocks.text: Notice a small pattern that saves a lot of memorizing: verbs ending in **-a** are almost always native Bantu verbs and follow the "-a becomes -i" negative rule (*kusoma → sisomi*). Verbs ending in **-i**, **-e** or **-u** are almost always Arabic loans (*kufikiri*, *kusamehe*, *kujibu*) and **keep their ending** in the negative: *sifikiri*, *sijibu*.

You have just finished twenty units and hold a complete A1 foundation: six subject prefixes, five tense slots, six noun classes, and enough vocabulary to get through a whole day in Dar es Salaam without switching to English. This is the right question to ask now: what turns A1 into A2?
Three things that will lift your level most

**1. The noun classes you haven't touched yet.** This course sets up six classes that cover over ninety percent of everyday sentences. The rest — the place class (*mahali*), the *ku-* class for verbs used as nouns, and the wider *u-* class — will feel easy because you already know the pattern: one sound, spreading through the whole sentence.

**2. Extensions that change a verb's meaning.** Swahili adds extensions to the end of a verb to change its meaning, and this is what makes speakers sound grown-up: *kupika* (to cook) → *kupikia* (to cook for someone) → *kupikwa* (to be cooked) → *kupikiana* (to cook for each other). One root, many meanings, without memorizing a single new word.

**3. Connectors that join long sentences.** *Ambaye/ambao* (who; which), *ili* (so that), *ingawa* (although), *kwa hivyo* (therefore). At A1 your sentences stand alone; at A2 they start to link up, and the difference is instantly audible.
What to do this week

Redo units 1 to 5 in one sitting. You'll be surprised how easy they are now — and that surprise is part of the method. After that: look up Bongo Flava songs (Tanzanian pop) with their lyrics, watch Swahili news broadcasts with slow, clear delivery, or follow Tanzanian social media accounts that use short sentences.

And find someone to talk to. Swahili is one of the world's big languages whose speakers are most patient with beginners, because almost everyone in East Africa also learned it as a second language. Your first sentence won't be perfect. It will still be answered with a smile and a *karibu*.
*Safari njema* — have a good journey.
